Whether the filer could potentially have qualifying earned income that can be used to qualify for the CDCC. ON A JOINT RETURN THIS IS AN <All> OF TWO PER-SPOUSE TESTS, because §21(d)(1) caps qualifying expenses at the SMALLER of the two spouses' earned incomes — a spouse with no earned income makes that minimum zero, so the credit is refused outright rather than merely limited. A tracked issue gave the secondary arm the self-employment term it never had: while Schedule C was primary-filer-only and a spouse's box-14A K-1 was knocked out, a secondary filer could have no self-employment earned income, so wages/combat pay/student-or-disabled was the whole of her test. Two tracked issues ended both, and a spouse whose only earned income was her own business failed this gate — the severest reach of a tracked issue, because it zeroes the credit BEFORE any earned-income limitation is computed. The primary arms likewise now read HIS own figure rather than the return-level total, which had counted HER business income toward HIS eligibility. SCOPE NOTE — this screen deliberately keeps reading the ZERO-FLOORED per-filer self-employment facts while the Form 2441 AMOUNT lines moved to the unfloored siblings. Two reasons, stated rather than assumed: (a) the arms below are > 0 TESTS, and a floored 0 and a negative both fail > 0, so this fact's value is identical under either input on every return; (b) the screen is structurally an <Any> over separate sources, not a SUM, so it cannot net a self-employment loss against wages at all. The residual that (b) leaves is real and disclosed: a filer whose self-employment LOSS exceeds his wages has a true Form 2441 earned income of zero, yet passes this screen on the wages arm. It is HARMLESS rather than merely unlikely — income:/cdccPrimaryEarnedIncomeWithCombatPayForCredits now floors that filer's line 4 at 0, and §21(d)(1)'s earned-income limitation then caps qualifying expenses at 0, so the credit is 0 whether or not the screen admitted him. Restructuring the <Any> into a summed earned-income test is NOT done here: it would pull the combat-pay election (deliberately Incomplete while undecided) into an eligibility gate, and it changes no value. COMPLETENESS, stated rather than claimed away: adding the secondary self-employment term gives that <Any> a Schedule-C-derived dependency it did not previously have, so in the two mid-interview states named on scheduleC:/scheduleCBelongsToSecondaryFiler (an answered /scheduleCFiler with /filingStatus unanswered; MFJ selected before the spouse exists in /filers) this fact resolves Placeholder(false) where it previously resolved Complete(false). The VALUE is unchanged in both, no committed scenario reaches either, and it self-heals once /filingStatus is answered — but it is a new demotion class, not a free addition.
STATUTORY EMPLOYEE ADD-BACK. All three wage arms now read income:/primaryFilerEarnedIncomeBaseWithStatutoryEmployeeWages and its secondary twin instead of the raw income:/*EmployerIncomeSubtotalBase. Round 7 routes a statutory employee's box 1 to the linked Schedule C's line 1, which takes it out of the raw base; Form 2441's Earned Income list adds it back at item 3 ("If you are filing Schedule C (Form 1040) as a statutory employee, the amount shown on line 1 of the schedule", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 4). This gate asks whether a filer HAD earned income, and a statutory employee whose only earnings are those wages HAS it: on the raw base this screen would answer false and refuse the whole credit before any earned-income limitation was computed. Complete safe and equal to the base on every committed return, none of which checks box 13.

Fact.Name: Filer has Qualifying Expenses CDCC
Fact.Description:
Whether the filer has any qualifying expenses for the Child and Dependent Care Credit. This is for the credit section, which means that they cannot include excluded benefits.
QUESTION TEXT: "In 2025, did you pay for the care of a qualifying person, or for household services, so that you (and your spouse, if filing jointly) could work or look for work?"
HELP TEXT: The purpose of the expense must be to let you work; an expense is not work related merely because you had it while you were working. A babysitter while you and your spouse go out to eat is not normally a work-related expense (Pub. 503 lines 412-420). Actively looking for work counts as work, but if you did not find a job and had no earned income for the year you cannot take the credit (Pub. 503 lines 407-410; i2441 lines 143-146). Unpaid volunteer work, or work for a nominal salary, is not work (Pub. 503 lines 428-430). Household services, such as a cook, maid, babysitter, housekeeper or cleaning person, count when they are at least partly for the well-being and protection of the qualifying person (Pub. 503, Household Services, lines 489-500 of the right column). If you worked or looked for work during only part of the period the care covered, only the expenses for that part count: $250 a month of care with 2 and a half months of work gives $625 (Pub. 503 lines 432-440). If you work part-time, figure the expenses for each day you worked (Pub. 503, Part-time work, right column from line 408). The per-person amounts asked next should hold only that work-related part.
ASKED WHEN: /maybeEligibleForCdcc is true, before the per-person expense amounts.
FEEDS: /cdccMaybeHasQualifyingExpenses, which opens the per-person expense questions.

Fact.Name: Was this care provider your household employee in 2025?
Fact.Description:
The Form 2441 line 1 column (d) attestation, PER CARE PROVIDER: "Was the care provider your household employee in 2025? For example, this generally includes nannies but not daycare centers" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1, the column head, with the Yes/No boxes at lines 29, 31 and 33). It is an attestation and not a derivation because the test the instructions state is a control test no fact graph can compute from a number: "If you pay someone to come to your home and care for your dependent or spouse and you can control not only what work is done but how it is done, that person is probably a household employee" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3).
UNANSWERED IS THE NORMAL STATE, NOT AN ERROR. No intake asks this today (the intake surface is SERVICE-owned, invariant #7), so this writable is Incomplete on every existing return and ../isHouseholdEmployee falls back to its shipping mirror. Nothing here is added to /cdccCareProviders/*/isComplete or /cdccCareProvidersIsComplete: making the question mandatory would turn every already-collected care provider incomplete, which is a far worse failure than the mirror this replaces.

Fact.Name: Is a Household Employee
Fact.Description:
Whether care provider is a household employee. Form 2441 line 1, column (d).
TWO ARMS, AND THE SECOND IS NOW A PLAIN FALSE. Arm 1 takes this provider's own ../writableIsHouseholdEmployee when it is answered; arm 2, for a provider whose question was never asked, answers No.
ARM 2 USED TO BE THE RETURN-LEVEL MIRROR, and retiring it was one of the three changes the successor contract required (2026-08-03, the Schedule H landing). It was a bare Dependency on /flowKnockoutHouseholdEmployee, which is now DERIVED from these very attestations: a mirror of a fact derived from this fact is a mirror of itself, and the graph would not have loaded. The retirement is not merely a cycle-break, though. The mirror printed the return's single yes/no in EVERY provider's column (d), including the daycare centre the form's own example says is not a household employee; it was tolerable only because the flag carried a submission block, so a true value was unfilable. The moment Schedule H made such a return filable, the mirror became a wrong answer on a filed Form 2441 — which is precisely why the contract said the two changes had to land together or not at all.
WHY FALSE IS THE RIGHT UNANSWERED ANSWER, stated rather than assumed. Column (d) is a per-provider attestation no intake asks today (invariant #7). False is what the shipping mirror already resolved to on every return that could actually file, so nothing observable moves; it keeps the field complete rather than turning every collected care provider Incomplete; and the direction it could be wrong in — a household employee reported as "No" — is caught upstream by scheduleH:/knockoutHouseholdEmployeeWithoutScheduleHAnswers only when SOME provider is attested Yes. A filer with a household-employee provider who answers nothing at all is the residual, and it is the same residual Schedule H line A carries; it is named on that knockout rather than hidden here.
WHAT THE MIRROR GOT WRONG, and why a rebody rather than prose. The shipping body was not a determination at all: it reported the FLOW's return-level "do you have a household employee" knockout flag in a PER-PROVIDER column. That is invisible on a filed return, because any true answer to the flag already carries BlockSubmissionOnTrue through flow:/flowIsKnockedOut, so the mirror could only ever resolve FALSE on a return that files. It is visible the moment the flag is true: EVERY provider's column (d) reads Yes, including the daycare centre the form's own example says is not one ("For example, this generally includes nannies but not daycare centers", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1). The node test that used to pin exactly that return was cdcc-household-employee-mirror-arm; with the mirror retired on 2026-08-03 it was renamed to cdcc-household-employee-unanswered-defaults-no and rewritten to pin the replacement default (both providers unanswered now read No rather than inheriting a return-level Yes). Its former assertions are in git history at that path.
THE REFUSAL IS RETIRED, AS OF 2026-08-03, AND THIS PARAGRAPH USED TO SAY IT MUST NOT BE. It read: "/flowKnockoutHouseholdEmployee stays a Writable, stays read by /dependentCareBenefitsIsComplete, and stays a submission block, because a filer with a household employee may owe employment taxes on Schedule H ... and Schedule H is not modelled anywhere in this graph." Every clause of that was true when written and the last one is what changed: dictionary/ty2025/scheduleH.xml now computes the tax and reaches Schedule 2 line 9, so the caution the paragraph rested on — "If the care provider is your household employee, you may owe employment taxes. For details, see the Instructions for Schedule H (Form 1040)" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1) — is answered by a computation rather than by a refusal. The flag is now Derived from these attestations, is no longer read by /dependentCareBenefitsIsComplete, and is no longer a member of flow:/flowIsKnockedOut.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Boolean, no rounding. Unanswered resolves FALSE, which is the same value the retired mirror resolved to on every return that could actually file, so the shipping value is unchanged.

If so, enter 'LAFCP' (Living Abroad Foreign Care Provider) in the space for the care provider's taxpayer identification number" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3, left column). Fact.Name: Care provider is a barred related individual
Fact.Description:
Screen: "Was this care provider your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child, or someone you (or your spouse, if filing jointly) can claim as a dependent?" A second sentence covers the taxpayer's own child: "If your child (including a stepchild or foster child) provided the care, answer Yes unless they were age 19 or older by the end of 2025 AND you cannot claim them as a dependent." Help text paraphrases i2441's own caution: "Don't list an ineligible related individual as a care provider on line 1. No credit is allowed for any amount paid to your spouse, the parent of your qualifying child, or a person whom you can claim as a dependent. If your child (including stepchild or foster child) provided the care, they must have been age 19 or older by the end of the year and they can't be your dependent" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3, restated at lines 73-77).
ASKED WHEN: for every provider in /cdccCareProviders (Part I is completed whenever providers are collected).
UNANSWERED: no safe default exists — an unanswered provider cannot be shown to be outside IRC 21(e)(6)'s bar, and the amount paid to a barred provider is disqualified from the credit entirely (not merely reduced), which this graph has no per-provider dollar-netting path for (the credit is computed from the per-qualifying-person attested amounts, not summed from this collection — see /cdccCareProvidersWithDueDiligenceReasons's sibling note). "Yes": the return is refused (/knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider) until the provider is corrected or removed — a data-completeness/eligibility refusal, not a computed netting, because the graph cannot safely determine which dollars to remove from an aggregate that was never itemized by provider. "No": no effect.
IMPORTANT — CLEARING THIS SCREEN DOES NOT, BY ITSELF, REMOVE THE DISALLOWED DOLLARS: this collection carries no link to the qualifying-person expense total the credit is actually computed from, so answering No (or deleting this provider) only clears the refusal — if you keep the same dollar amount, you must ALSO separately reduce the qualifying person's own expense amount by whatever you paid this barred provider, or the disallowed amount remains inside the credit.
Validation: Boolean; no Limit. Feeds /knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider.

Fact.Name: Refusal for a barred related provider whose dollars are not yet allocated (IRC 21(e)(6))
Fact.Description:
At least one care provider is attested to be barred under IRC 21(e)(6) — the filer's spouse, the parent of the qualifying child, a person the filer or spouse can claim as a dependent, or the filer's own under-19 child — AND at least one qualifying person or qualifying filer with care expenses has not said how much of those expenses was paid to that provider.
WHAT THIS FACT USED TO SAY, quoted so the withdrawal can be checked rather than taken: "No credit is allowed for any amount paid to such a provider, and this graph computes the credit from the per-qualifying-person attested totals rather than by summing this provider collection, so there is no dollar this fact can subtract — the refusal is the correct residue until the return is corrected." THE SECOND CLAUSE IS THE ONE THAT WAS FALSE, and the lead's 2026-09-12 ruling on row 13 of the EXT-BLOCK8 integration audit is what withdrew it: the printed caution is an arithmetic instruction about dollars ("No credit is allowed for any amount paid to your spouse ...", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 3) and says nothing about declining to file, so refusing where a netting is available was a deferral wearing a verdict's clothes.
WHAT NOW NETS. /familyAndHousehold/*/writableCdccBarredProviderExpensesStillIncluded and its /filers/*/ twin ask, per qualifying person, how much of THAT person's line 2 column (d) amount was paid to the barred provider, and /familyAndHousehold/*/cdccQualifyingExpenseAmount subtracts it. The subtraction lands in the column (d) wrapper, so it reaches the more-than-three RANKING and the printed rows and line 30 and the MeF export, not just the credit total — a person whose expenses were mostly paid to a barred provider stops out-ranking a person whose were not.
WHY THE ALLOCATION IS ASKED PER PERSON RATHER THAN NETTED FROM THE PROVIDER. The provider row carries a gross payment (/cdccCareProviders/*/amountPaidForCare) with no link to the qualifying person it bought care for, and that payment can also contain dollars outside the credit entirely. Subtracting it from an arbitrary person would delete allowed dollars. This is shape (ii) of the two the contract offered, chosen for that reason.
WHY A REFUSAL SURVIVES AT ALL, AND WHY IT IS NOW A CORRECT ONE. The allocation is an attestation, so it can be blank — and blank is not $0: a $0 default would leave the disallowed dollars inside the credit with nothing on the return saying so. The residue is a data-completeness guard whose discharge is the FILER ANSWERING, which is what REFUSAL-VERDICTS.md reserves the correct-refusal verdict for, and it is a strictly smaller population than the one this fact used to refuse. The contract's own closing note said the node would be DELETED when the netting landed; it is narrowed instead, because that note assumed shape (i), an exact provider-to-person link with nothing left to ask.
THE OTHER TWO EXITS STILL WORK and are the ones the printed caution names first: remove the barred provider from line 1, or correct the return so no provider is barred.

Fact.Name: Care provider was a dependent care center that did not comply with state and local regulations
Fact.Description:
Screen: "Was this provider a dependent care center that did NOT follow all of the state and local rules that apply to it?" Answer Yes only if BOTH are true: the provider is a dependent care center, and it did not comply.
HELP TEXT: "A dependent care center is a place that provides care for more than six persons (other than persons who live there) and receives a fee, payment, or grant for providing services for any of those persons, even if the center isn't run for profit" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 2). "You can count care provided outside your home by a dependent care center only if the center complies with all state and local regulations that apply to these centers" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 7). A babysitter, a nanny, a relative, a day camp or any other provider that is not a centre is a No. A centre that follows the rules is a No. If you are not sure whether the centre is licensed or registered as your state or locality requires, ask the centre — this is the centre's own compliance, not yours.
ASKED WHEN: for every provider in /cdccCareProviders, alongside the barred-related-provider question (../writableIsBarredRelatedProvider) that shares this fact's shape and its reason.
UNANSWERED: no refusal and no netting — /knockoutCdccNoncompliantDependentCareCenter is IsComplete-first and resolves false, exactly as ../writableIsBarredRelatedProvider's knockout does, so an unanswered provider neither refuses the return nor makes the credit Incomplete. The application should carry this as a required screen on the provider card; the graph cannot make it one without refusing every return that has not reached the card (ruling 6). "Yes": the return is refused (/knockoutCdccNoncompliantDependentCareCenter) until the provider is corrected or removed.
IMPORTANT — CLEARING THIS SCREEN DOES NOT, BY ITSELF, REMOVE THE DISALLOWED DOLLARS, for the same reason ../writableIsBarredRelatedProvider states: this collection carries no link to the qualifying person whose expenses the credit is computed from, so the amount paid to a noncompliant centre has to be taken out of that person's own expense amount by hand.
Validation: Boolean; no Limit. Feeds /knockoutCdccNoncompliantDependentCareCenter.

Fact.Name: Refusal for a noncompliant dependent care center (IRC 21(b)(2)(C))
Fact.Description:
At least one care provider is attested to be a dependent care center that does not comply with the state and local regulations that apply to it. Expenses for services provided outside the taxpayer's household by such a center are not taken into account at all.
WHY A REFUSAL AND NOT A SUBTRACTION — NO **SAFE** SUBTRACTION, NOT NO COMPUTABLE ONE. [CORRECTED 2026-09-17, FIX pass, review finding M-1. This paragraph previously said the credit is computed from per-person totals "so there is no dollar this fact can subtract". That reason is FALSE and was measured false: /cdccCareProviders/*/amountPaidForCare is Form 2441 column (e) and exists; /cdccUncappedQualifyingExpenses (line 30) is a plain Add of two CollectionSums; and /cdccQualifyingExpenseCap (line 27) switches on /cdccCountOfQualifyingPersons — it is return-level, by person count, not per-person. A noncompliant centre's column-(e) dollar could therefore be subtracted from line 30 WITHOUT any provider-to-person link.] The refusal stands on the real reason: column (e) is the GROSS amount paid to the provider, and column (d) is only what was incurred AND paid in 2025 and net of the line 28 benefits. The two are not the same dollars, so a filer who already kept the centre's disallowed payments out of column (d) — or who paid the centre for 2024-incurred or benefit-funded care — would have that money subtracted a second time. The subtraction is structurally available and would OVER-SUBTRACT a compliant filer, the same standard that rejects a coherence knockout on the column (d) intakes. Refusal is the correct residue until the return is corrected (the centre removed, or the amount paid to it excluded from the qualifying-person totals that do feed the credit). Same shape and the same residue as /knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider.

Fact.Name: Refusal for out-of-home care that fails the 8-hour test (IRC 21(b)(2)(B))
Fact.Description:
At least one qualifying person who is not a dependent child under 13 had some of their care provided outside the taxpayer's household and does not regularly spend at least 8 hours a day in that household. IRC 21(b)(2)(B) does not let the out-of-home part of those expenses be taken into account at all.
WHY A REFUSAL AND NOT A SUBTRACTION. The expense intake asks one amount for the whole of a person's care (familyAndHousehold:/familyAndHousehold/*/writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount, filers:/filers/*/writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount) and nothing in the graph splits it between care given in the home and care given outside it. Zeroing the person's whole amount would delete the in-home care the statute allows; leaving it would allow the out-of-home care the statute forbids. There is no third number to compute from, so the refusal is the correct residue until the return is corrected. Same reasoning, and the same shape, as /knockoutCdccBarredRelatedProvider.
HOW THE FILER CLEARS IT, AND WHY THAT IS NOW TRUE. [CORRECTED 2026-09-17, FIX pass, review finding H-1. This paragraph previously promised "the filer reduces that person's expense amount to the in-home part" while this fact reads NO DOLLAR — reducing the amount changed none of the flag's conjuncts, so the promised remedy did not clear the refusal and the only exit was a false answer to the location question. The mechanism, not the promise, is what changed.] The location attestation is scoped to the amount entered — "Was any of the care INCLUDED IN THE AMOUNT YOU ENTERED for this person provided somewhere other than your home?" — so the two honest exits are: (1) reduce that person's column (d) entry to the in-home part, after which the location answer is truthfully No and the 8-hour question is never reached; or (2) answer that the person does regularly spend at least 8 hours a day in the home. A person with no qualifying expenses at all (../cdccHasQualifyingExpenses false) is never refused: that conjunct is in both per-person flags, IsComplete-guarded.
COMPLETE-SAFE: each per-person flag is IsComplete-first, so an unanswered attestation neither refuses nor makes anything Incomplete (ruling 6).

The harmless half landed first, on purpose; the coupled half landed against it.

Fact.Name: Primary filer's dependent care benefit from their own sole proprietorship or partnership
Fact.Description:
The amount the PRIMARY filer received in 2025 under a dependent care assistance program of their own sole proprietorship or partnership. Form 2441 line 12 asks for it in as many words — "If you were self-employed or a partner, include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 2) — and until this fill no writable in the graph could carry one, which is why line 22 ("Is any amount on line 12 or 13 from your sole proprietorship or partnership?", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 2) was a hardcoded False.
WHY IT IS AN ATTESTATION AND NOT A DERIVATION. Section 129(e)(4) makes "an individual who owns the entire interest in an unincorporated trade or business ... his own employer" and makes "a partnership ... the employer of each partner who is an employee within the meaning of paragraph (3)" (26 U.S.C. 129, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section129&num=0&edition=2024), and paragraph (3) pulls a section 401(c)(1) self-employed individual into the term "employee" (26 U.S.C. 129, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section129&num=0&edition=2024). So the amount is a real employer-plan payment — but it is paid under a plan the graph does not model, is not reported on any information return this graph reads (box 10 is a Form W-2 field and a proprietor issues himself no Form W-2), and cannot be recovered from Schedule C's gross receipts or expense total. It is a filer fact, exactly as /familyAndHousehold/*/writableCdccQualifyingExpenseAmount is.
SIGN/ROUNDING: Dollar, non-negative by declared Limit, rounded to whole dollars by /cdccPrimaryFilerSelfEmployedDependentCareBenefits, which is the fact everything downstream reads. Unanswered is $0 there, never a Placeholder.
interpretation:provisional — CHOSEN READING: the attestation is NOT conditioned on the graph holding a Schedule C or a partnership K-1 for this filer. REJECTED: gating it on scheduleC:/scheduleCBelongsToPrimaryFiler or a scheduleE K-1 test, so that an answer from a filer with no modelled business resolves to $0. Rejected on DIRECTION: a gate that is wrong in either direction silently DROPS an answered benefit out of line 12, which shrinks line 26 taxable benefits dollar for dollar and UNDER-states income — the taxpayer-favourable direction this repo treats most seriously — whereas an un-gated attestation can only be wrong if the filer answers a question the intake should not have asked, and that error over-states line 12. The population is also wider than a modelled Schedule C: section 129(e)(4) reaches partners, whose businesses arrive here as Schedule E K-1s, and a filer can have a plan in a year the business runs at zero profit. Which filers are asked is a SERVICE-owned intake question (invariant #7).

Fact.Name: Secondary filer's dependent care benefit from their own sole proprietorship or partnership
Fact.Description:
The SECONDARY (MFJ spouse) filer's mirror of /writablePrimaryFilerSelfEmployedDependentCareBenefits, which carries the full statement of why this is an attestation and why it is not gated on a modelled business. Per filer and not per return because section 129's exclusion is computed for an EMPLOYEE — "Gross income of an employee does not include amounts paid or incurred by the employer for dependent care assistance provided to such employee" (26 U.S.C. 129, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section129&num=0&edition=2024) — and because the graph's line-21 plan maximum, its line-18/19 earned-income limitation and its taxable-benefit allocator are all per filer already.
NO secondaryFilerUsedWithoutMFJ CONSISTENCY GUARD, deliberately and disclosed rather than silently absent. A filer who answers this on an MFJ return and then switches to single, HOH or MFS leaves a stale answer behind. Line 12 and line 22 both ignore it — their MFJ Switch takes the primary alone on every other status, and tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-line22-non-mfj-stale-secondary-answer is drawn to be exactly that shape and pins line 22 at the primary's 2,000 rather than the 3,500 sum. What the stale answer DOES still reach is /hasReportedSecondaryFilerDependentCareBenefits, which turns true and opens a plan-maximum question for a spouse who is not on the return. That is the same hazard class seven other modules guard with BlockSubmissionOnTrue and that scheduleC:/scheduleCFiler explicitly declines to guard — "a THIRD form's worth of submission-blocking behaviour change riding on an attribution unit; it belongs with the K-1 one, in a unit that does both." The same reasoning applies here: adding the guard is its own unit, and adding a filing-status conjunct to this chain instead would drag filingStatus completeness into a fact that is deliberately dependency-free when unanswered (see /cdccSelfEmployedDependentCareBenefitsAmount's outer gate).

Fact.Name: Self-employed dependent care benefits included in Form 2441 line 12
Fact.Description:
The portion of Form 2441 line 12 that came from a sole proprietorship or a partnership — the return-level total this graph puts on line 22.
THE MFJ SWITCH IS /cdccDependentCareBenefitsAmount's, DELIBERATELY IDENTICAL. Line 22 asks about "any amount on line 12 or 13", so this fact must sum exactly the filers line 12 sums and no others: on a joint return both spouses' amounts, otherwise the primary filer's alone. A return-level sum that included a spouse's amount on a status where line 12 does not would put more on line 22 than line 12 contains, and line 23 (line 15 less line 22) would then subtract money that was never added.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER, stated because line 22's own words are wider than this fact. Line 22 reaches an amount on line 12 OR ON LINE 13, and line 13 is the grace-period carryover (/cdccCarryoverAmountFromPriorTaxYear), a single return-level writable that does not record whose plan it came from. A filer whose 2024 carryover came from their own proprietorship's plan therefore gets a line 22 that is UNDER-stated by that carryover. Direction: line 23 is correspondingly OVER-stated, so line 26 taxable benefits is over-stated — taxpayer-ADVERSE, the safe direction — while line 24 deductible benefits is under-stated, which this graph does not route to any deduction (see /cdccDeductibleBenefitsAmount). Splitting the carryover writable by plan is a SERVICE-side intake question shape (invariant #7) before it is a dictionary edit. [2026-08-24, unit cdcc-benefits-distribution: that intake now EXISTS - /writableCdccCarryoverAmountAllocatedToPrimaryFiler - but it splits the carryover BY SPOUSE, not BY PLAN KIND, so THIS gap is untouched: line 22 is still under-stated by a sole-proprietorship carryover, in the taxpayer-adverse direction stated above. The two are different questions and the new writable must not be read as answering this one. The same overlap is why /cdccBenefitsAttributionIsAttested refuses a spouse whose attributed forfeiture exceeds their box 10 plus their attributed carryover: there, line 14 and line 22 can be drawing on the same dollars and no printed line says which.]
NO CAP AT LINE 15, DELIBERATELY. If the line-14 forfeiture exceeds the non-self-employed part of line 12, line 22 can exceed line 15 and line 23 goes negative. The form prints no floor on line 23 and no cap on line 22, and inventing a LesserOf here would be arithmetic no source states; line 26's own "If zero or less, enter -0-" absorbs the consequence (/cdccTaxableBenefits already floors at $0). Recorded rather than papered over.
THE OUTER GATE IS LINE 22'S OWN "No. Enter -0-." BRANCH, and it is also what keeps this fill additions-only. Both attestation wrappers resolve $0 with no dependency on anything else, so a return that answers neither takes the bare $0 arm and never evaluates the filing status. Without the gate this fact inherits filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFJ's completeness, and a scenario that leaves the filing status unanswered would see line 22 — a fact that was a hardcoded $0 with no dependencies at all — turn Placeholder. California TY2025 reads this fact through its stateSystems export (FTB 3506 Part III dependent care benefits).

If you were self-employed or a partner, include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 2) — and the second term is new with the line-22 fill. Fact.Name: Form 2441 line B — deemed income of $250 or $500 a month is entered on this return
Fact.Description:
Form 2441's line B checkbox: "If you or your spouse was a student or was disabled during 2025 and you're entering deemed income of $250 or $500 a month on Form 2441 based on the income rules listed in the instructions under If You or Your Spouse Was a Student or Disabled, check this box" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/f2441.pdf, page 1). The instructions restate it as an obligation rather than an option: "If you enter deemed income of $250 or $500 a month on Form 2441, you must check the box on Form 2441, line B" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 4).
IT BECAME A GAP THE MOMENT DEEMED INCOME BECAME ENTERABLE. Before frontier pack 1 no fact in this graph could put a deemed amount on the form, so an absent line B was correct by construction. Four bodies can enter one now — Form 2441 lines 18 and 19 (the Part III pair pack 1 rebodied) and lines 4 and 5 (the credit pair the day-1 fill rebodied) — and this checkbox is their required companion.
ALL FOUR ARE READ, NOT THE PART III PAIR ALONE. The trigger is "if you enter deemed income ... on Form 2441", not "on Part III", and a return whose line 5 took the deemed operand while its line 19 did not still owes the box. The two pairs' arm-1 GUARDS are identical, but their sums read DIFFERENT combat-pay siblings hanging off two SEPARATE writable elections, which the instruction contemplates in as many words ("You can elect to include your nontaxable combat pay in earned income when figuring your credit, even if you elect not to include it in earned income for the ... exclusion or deduction for child and dependent care benefits", https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 4) — so a deemed amount falling between the two sums binds on one pair only. Reading all four is correct whether or not this graph's gates can actually reach that split, and it is the cheaper default.
THE PREDICATE IS "THE LINE TOOK THE DEEMED OPERAND", read off the resolved line rather than recomputed. Each of the four lines is GreaterOf(that filer's actual sum, the deemed product, $0) under a guard of All(joint return, IsComplete over the deemed product, months > 0). Under that guard the line is never BELOW the deemed product, so "line is less than or equal to the deemed product" is exactly "the line equals it", i.e. the deemed operand is what got entered. The alternative — re-deriving each filer's actual wage + combat-pay + self-employment sum here and comparing — would put a fifth and sixth copy of an expression that already exists twice per filer into the tree, and the copies would drift.
interpretation:provisional — CHOSEN READING: the EXACT TIE (deemed product equal to the actual sum) checks the box. REJECTED: requiring the deemed product to STRICTLY exceed the actual sum. Rejected on direction and on the instruction's own words: on a tie the filer computed the line under the section 21(d)(2) rule and the amount they entered IS the deemed $250 or $500 a month, so the "you must check the box" trigger is met; and line B is a DISCLOSURE that moves no dollar, so checking it on a tie can over-claim nothing, while omitting it disobeys an express instruction. Witnessed by tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-line-b-deemed-equals-actual-tie, which is drawn to be exactly that shape (four months at $250 against $1,000 of actual wages).
THE MeF ELEMENT NAME IS NOT DECLARED HERE, ON PURPOSE. This repo owns the fact graph, not the MeF binding (invariant #7); inventing an element name is how a wrong one ships. Export mef is declared and the binding is left to the surface that owns it, exactly as /cdccCheckboxSoleProprietorshipYes and /cdccShouldIncludeMoreThanThreeCareProviders are.
THE GUARD GAINED A FOURTH CONJUNCT ON 2026-08-05 WITH THE FOUR ARMS' OWN, and it had to. This fact does not re-derive each filer's actual sum; it asks whether the RESOLVED line is at or below that filer's deemed product, which is equivalent to "the deemed operand is what got entered" ONLY while this guard and the arms' guard agree. Obligation (f) added income:/cdccPrimaryFilerIsStudentOrQualifyingIndividual (and its twin) to all four arms — section 21(d)(2) reaches "a spouse who is a student or a qualifying individual described in subsection (b)(1)(C)" — so without the same conjunct here a return with months answered but NEITHER limb would take the arms' fallthrough, where the actual line may sit BELOW the product, and this box would be checked on a return entering no deemed dollar at all. That is not hypothetical: tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-months-without-student-status-refused is exactly that return and asserted a true box until this commit. The boundary pair cdcc-deemed-disabled-spouse-abode-satisfied-deems / cdcc-deemed-disabled-spouse-abode-unapplied pins both polarities on one input.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Boolean; no rounding. False on every return that leaves filers:/filers/*/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool unanswered — which is every scenario in the corpus — so this fact is additive.
REACHABLE ON A FILED RETURN — this paragraph was FALSE and is corrected (pre-PR fg-review, 2026-07-31). It used to say cdcc:/knockoutStudentOrDisabled "refuses the MFJ population that reaches the four arms, so a true line B is correct-but-unreachable on a filed return". That refusal's credits gate is a STRICT GreaterThan against /cdccQualifyingExpenseCap, and full-year deeming lands EXACTLY on the cap, so it evaporates on exactly the returns that deem most. A single deemed spouse whose deemed amount reaches the cap files, and this box is checked on their Form 2441 — which is what the instruction requires. What is refused is the BOTH-spouses shape, by /knockoutBothSpousesDeemedStudentOrDisabled, and that refusal exists because section 21(d)(2)'s flush text restricts the deeming, not because line B is doubtful.

Fact.Name: Months in which BOTH spouses were a student or unable to care for themselves
Fact.Description:
THE MONTH-IDENTITY INTAKE section 21(d)(2)'s flush text needs, modelled under the BUILD-FIRST directive. The flush text restricts the deeming rule to "only one spouse for any one month" (26 U.S.C. 21, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section21&num=0&edition=2024), restated for a reader as "If, in the same month, both you and your spouse were either students or disabled, only one of you can be treated as having earned income in that month under these rules" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 4).
WHY A COUNT OF OVERLAPPED MONTHS AND NOT TWELVE MONTH FLAGS, which is the whole design decision and the reason this was buildable at all. The restriction is about SIMULTANEITY, not about WHICH calendar month: nothing in section 21(d)(2) or in i2441 turns on whether the shared month was March or September. So the only datum the rule needs beyond the two existing per-filer counts is how many months they SHARED. Writing filers:/filers/*/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool as twelve Booleans would carry eleven bits of information the statute never reads, and would migrate a writable 1,296 persisted stores answer. One Int is the whole missing intake.
THE PRIOR CONTRACT CALLED THIS SURFACE UNBUILDABLE AND THAT WAS THE ONE THING TO RE-DERIVE. Under the BUILD-FIRST directive a blocked-on-a-SERVICE-screen ground is dispatchable — the dictionary declares the writable, the application builds the screen against it — and the re-derivation above shrinks what has to be declared from twelve flags to one count.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Int, months, 0 to 12 inclusive by declared Limit; no rounding. It is UNANSWERED on every scenario and every node-test fixture except the ones this unit authored, so it is Incomplete corpus-wide and both of its readers, /cdccDeemedMonthsDoNotOverlap and /cdccOverlappedMonthsValidlyAllocated, are complete-safe against that.
WHAT IT DOES NOT DO, AND WHO DOES IT NOW. It does not, on its own, allocate the shared months. It makes exactly one thing decidable that was not: whether there is anything to allocate at all. THE SENTENCE THAT FOLLOWED WAS TRUE FOR HALF A DAY AND IS RETIRED: it called the allocation "the remaining half of the contract", living one module over. Lane CD3 landed it the same day — /cdccOverlappedMonthsAllocatedToPrimaryFiler is the taxpayer's choice of which spouse takes the shared months, /cdccOverlappedMonthsValidlyAllocated proves the answer set describes a real calendar, and income:/primaryFilerDeemedMonthsAfterOverlapAllocation and its twin apply the split to all four Form 2441 earned-income lines through the two deemed products.

Fact.Name: The two spouses' student-or-disabled months are provably disjoint
Fact.Description:
True only when the return has ATTESTED a zero overlap AND the two per-filer month counts are arithmetically capable of being disjoint. This is the released condition for /knockoutBothSpousesDeemedStudentOrDisabled, and it is deliberately a PROOF rather than a report of the taxpayer's answer.
ALL THREE CONJUNCTS ARE LOAD-BEARING, and only the first is one an intake would have volunteered. (1) THE ATTESTATION: the overlap Int is answered, and it is zero. (2) THE ARITHMETIC POSSIBILITY. Answering "zero shared months" is not by itself consistent: a couple who were each a student for all twelve months CANNOT have shared none of them, and a graph that released them on their say-so would be releasing an impossible claim. Twelve months is the whole year, so disjointness requires /primaryFiler/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool plus /secondaryFiler/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool to be at most 12. (3) THE STATUS COHERENCE — added after the first cut of this fact was written without it, and it is the same class of check as (2). BOTH spouses must actually say they were a student or unable to care for themselves. Without it, a return answering six months each with isStudent AND isDisabled false on both filers was released, and it FILED WITH DEEMED DOLLARS: the deemed arms' own guard is All(MFJ, IsComplete(the product), months above zero) and carries NO isStudentOrDisabled term, so the products bind, while /specialEarnedIncomeFlowRequirementsSansIncomeAndFilingStatus — which is Any(the two filers' isStudentOrDisabled) and gates BOTH student/disabled refusal screens — is false, so /knockoutStudentOrDisabled could not fire either. That measurement is what put this conjunct here; the return is now REFUSED and is pinned by tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-months-without-student-status-refused. With all three, a true here means the flush text is SATISFIED on a coherently answered return — each spouse's deemed months are their own, no month is counted twice, and deeming both chains independently is exactly what section 21(d)(2) allows.
THE COMPARISON IS SPELLED Not(GreaterThan(x, 0)) AND Not(GreaterThan(sum, 12)) rather than with a LessThanOrEqual, because GreaterThan over Int is the form already proven in this module (/cdccEnteredDeemedIncomeForStudentOrDisabled compares a month count against <Int>0</Int>) and Add over Int is proven at /cdccQpExpensesRemain. A negative overlap answer is nonsense the Limit already refuses, and reading it as "no overlap" costs nothing because the sum bound still has to hold.
COMPLETE-SAFE BY CONSTRUCTION, AND THE CONJUNCT ORDER IS PART OF THE CONSTRUCTION. The three IsCompletes come first, so a return that leaves any of the three writables unanswered — which is every scenario in the corpus — resolves this fact FALSE and Complete rather than Incomplete, and the refusal it guards is unchanged corpus-wide. The two isStudentOrDisabled conjuncts are LAST for the same reason and it matters more for them: they are Derived from Writables this graph does not require every return to answer, so evaluating them first would make this fact Incomplete wherever isStudent and isDisabled are both unanswered — which would delete rows from the resolved surface rather than add one. The All short-circuits false on the unanswered-overlap IsComplete long before it reaches them. MEASURED rather than asserted: the delta capture after this conjunct landed still reports 0 removed and 0 changed with the same single added path.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Boolean; no rounding.

Fact.Name: How many of the SHARED student-or-disabled months are treated as the primary filer's
Fact.Description:
THE ALLOCATION CHOICE section 21(d)(2)'s flush text leaves to the taxpayer, modelled here. The flush text restricts the deeming rule to "only one spouse for any one month" (26 U.S.C. 21, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section21&num=0&edition=2024) and says NOTHING about WHICH spouse. Neither does the instruction: "If, in the same month, both you and your spouse were either students or disabled, only one of you can be treated as having earned income in that month under these rules" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 4). Pub. 503 says the same twice over and also declines to choose: "This rule applies to only one spouse for any 1 month. If, in the same month, both you and your spouse didn't work and are either full-time students or not physically or mentally able to care for yourselves, only one of you can be treated as having earned income in that month" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p503.pdf, page 4).
WHY AN ATTESTATION AND NOT A DERIVED RULE. The contract's obligation (b) asserted that "assigning every overlapped month to the LOWER-earning spouse maximises the credit". THAT IS FALSE, and two worked returns on the SAME statute flip which rule wins, which is why no rule is derivable:
CASE A (one qualifying person, $250 a month; both spouses students all twelve months, so all twelve are shared; primary earned $45,000, secondary $1,200; $6,000 of expenses — the shape of tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-both-spouses-knockout). Give ALL twelve shared months to the secondary: line 4 = max(45,000, 0) = 45,000, line 5 = max(1,200, 12 x 250 = 3,000) = 3,000, line 3 = 3,000, line 6 = 3,000. Split them six/six instead: line 5 = max(1,200, 1,500) = 1,500 and line 6 = 1,500. The EXTREME allocation wins by $1,500 of line-6 base, because the primary's deemed income was never binding.
CASE B (same statute; primary earned $100, secondary $0). All twelve to the secondary (the lower earner): line 4 = max(100, 0) = 100, line 5 = 3,000, line 6 = 100. Six/six: line 4 = 1,500, line 5 = 1,500, line 6 = 1,500. Now the BALANCED allocation wins, by fifteen times.
Line 6 takes the SMALLEST of lines 3, 4 and 5, so the taxpayer is maximising a minimum over a discrete parameter, and the maximiser is at an endpoint in case A and in the interior in case B. A graph that picked either rule would compute a number the statute does not require and would be wrong for half the population. The exclusion side makes it worse rather than better: lines 18 and 19 use a DIFFERENT combat-pay election and feed line 20, and a larger exclusion is not even reliably good for the filer (it removes the same dollars from /eitcEarnedIncomeBase, direction region-dependent — the statement is on income:/cdccEarnedIncomeSecondaryFilerPartIII). So "optimal" is not one number to aim at. The statute leaves the choice to the taxpayer; so does this fact. The graph enforces only what the statute enforces, in /cdccOverlappedMonthsValidlyAllocated.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Int, months, 0 to 12 inclusive by declared Limit; no rounding. The SEMANTIC bound is /cdccMonthsBothSpousesStudentOrDisabled, which is not expressible as a Limit against another fact, so it is a conjunct of the validity gate instead: an answer above the shared-month count leaves the return refused rather than silently clamped. UNANSWERED on every scenario and every node-test fixture except the ones this unit authored, so it is Incomplete corpus-wide and both of its readers are complete-safe against that.
THE SECONDARY FILER'S SHARE IS NOT A SECOND WRITABLE: it is the shared-month count less this answer, derived at income:/secondaryFilerDeemedMonthsAfterOverlapAllocation. Two writables could disagree with each other and with the overlap count; one cannot.

Fact.Name: The shared student-or-disabled months are validly allocated one spouse per month
Fact.Description:
True only when the return has answered BOTH month-overlap questions and the two answers, taken with the two per-filer month counts, describe a calendar that can actually exist. This is the released condition for the OVERLAPPING half of /knockoutBothSpousesDeemedStudentOrDisabled, and it is the switch that turns on the split in income:/primaryFilerDeemedMonthsAfterOverlapAllocation and its twin. Like its sibling /cdccDeemedMonthsDoNotOverlap it is a PROOF, not a report of what the taxpayer said.
WHAT IT PROVES, conjunct by conjunct. Write P and S for the two per-filer counts, V for the shared count and A for the share of V treated as the primary filer's. (1) ALL FOUR ANSWERS ARE PRESENT. Four IsCompletes, FIRST, so a return that leaves any of them unanswered — which is every scenario in the corpus — resolves this fact FALSE and Complete rather than Incomplete. (2) A IS AT MOST V. The taxpayer cannot hand the primary filer more shared months than they shared. An over-answer is REFUSED, not clamped: clamping would file a return whose deemed months the taxpayer never agreed to. (3) V IS AT MOST P AND AT MOST S. A month cannot be shared by two people unless each of them had it. This is the conjunct that catches "we shared three months" from a couple where one spouse reports none. (4) THE UNION FITS IN THE YEAR: P + S - V is at most 12, spelled as P + S at most V + 12 so that no Subtract is needed in a comparison. This generalises the sibling fact's arithmetic-possibility check, which is exactly this bound at V = 0. (5) BOTH SPOUSES ACTUALLY SAY they were a student or unable to care for themselves. Same conjunct, same reason, as /cdccDeemedMonthsDoNotOverlap's third: the four deemed arms' own guard is All(MFJ, IsComplete(the product), months above zero) and carries NO isStudentOrDisabled term, so without this a return with both statuses false would deem dollars while /knockoutStudentOrDisabled could not fire.
DELIBERATELY LAST, the two isStudentOrDisabled conjuncts, for the reason the sibling fact records: they are Derived from Writables this graph does not require every return to answer, so evaluating them first would make this fact Incomplete wherever isStudent and isDisabled are both unanswered — and this fact is read by the two allocated-month facts, which feed the two deemed products, which feed all four Form 2441 earned-income lines. An Incomplete here would DELETE resolved rows rather than add them.
WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE, stated so it is not mistaken for handled. It does not check that the allocation is the one that maximises anything; there is no such rule (see /cdccOverlappedMonthsAllocatedToPrimaryFiler). It does not reach the annual-versus-monthly deviation or the section 21(b)(1)(C) abode test, which are obligations (b) and (f) on /knockoutStudentOrDisabled and are unchanged by this unit.
AN INCOHERENT ANSWER SET FALLS BACK RATHER THAN CORRUPTING. A return answering P = 0, S = 6, V = 3 fails conjunct (3), this fact is false, both allocated-month facts return the raw per-filer counts, and the secondary filer is deemed her own six months — which is right, since with P = 0 there is nothing to share and nothing to allocate. The refusal is what stops the return, not the arithmetic.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Boolean; no rounding.

Fact.Name: Refusal for a joint return that deems income to BOTH spouses (IRC section 21(d)(2) flush text)
Fact.Description:
Refuses a joint return on which BOTH spouses answered the months-as-a-student-or- disabled question above zero. Section 21(d)(2) deems earned income to a student or incapable spouse and then restricts it in its flush text: "In the case of any husband and wife, this paragraph shall apply with respect to only one spouse for any one month" (26 U.S.C. 21, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-2024-title26-section21&num=0&edition=2024). Pub. 503 states the same rule for a reader: "Both spouses were students or disabled. If, in the same month, both you and your spouse were either students or disabled, only one of you can be treated as having earned income in that month under these rules" (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/i2441.pdf, page 4). This graph deems on BOTH chains independently and has no one-spouse-per-month term, so it computes a credit the statute denies. The refusal is the honest answer until the split exists.
WHY A NEW REFUSAL AND NOT A CONJUNCT ON /knockoutStudentOrDisabled — this is the whole finding, and it is arithmetic rather than opinion. That refusal is All(Any(the benefits gate, the credits gate), Any(primary made less, secondary made less)), and its credits gate is /showSpecialEarnedIncomeKnockoutFlowInCredits, which carries GreaterThan(/cdccQualifyingExpenseCap, /lowerOfCdccEarnedIncomeMfj). Deeming for the WHOLE YEAR produces 12 x $250 = $3,000 with one qualifying person and 12 x $500 = $6,000 with two or more — EXACTLY /cdccQualifyingExpenseCap in each case (/cdccMaxClaimableExpenseWithOneQP and -TwoQP). GreaterThan is strict, so at full-year deeming the gate is FALSE, the old refusal evaporates, and the return files. The population section 21(d)(2) restricts is therefore precisely the population the old refusal stops covering, and no conjunct added to it can reach them.
MEASURED DIVERGENCE, the fixture this ships with — tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-both-spouses-knockout, and every number below is ITS number. (This paragraph described a different, two-qualifying-person case with no actual earned income and a $600 divergence until 2026-08-03; that case was never the one that shipped, and the figures are re-derived here from the fixture and its transcript.) MFJ, ONE qualifying person, both spouses full-time students for all twelve months, $45,000 of W-2 wages on the primary filer and $1,200 on the secondary, $6,000 of expenses and no dependent care benefits. One qualifying person means $250 a month, so each chain independently deems 12 x $250 = $3,000. Line 4 = max($45,000 actual, $3,000 deemed) = $45,000, his actual winning; line 5 = max($1,200 actual, $3,000 deemed) = $3,000, the DEEMED winning and landing exactly on /cdccQualifyingExpenseCap, which is $3,000 for one qualifying person. Those values, the strict gate going false and /knockoutStudentOrDisabled evaporating to Complete false are what the assert file pins. THE DIVERGENCE ON THIS PARTICULAR FIXTURE IS ZERO, AND THE PARAGRAPH THAT USED TO STAND HERE SAID IT WAS $1,500 OF BASE AND $300 OF CREDIT — CORRECTED 2026-08-04 (loop-4 lane CD3, which had to derive the best legal allocation in order to model it). The retired text reasoned that "the best legal split is six months each", halving both deemed amounts to 6 x $250 = $1,500. SIX MONTHS EACH IS LEGAL BUT IT IS NOT THE BEST: giving the secondary filer ALL TWELVE shared months is equally legal — the flush text asks only that no month be counted for both spouses, not that the months be shared out — and it produces line 4 = max($45,000, $0) = $45,000, line 5 = max($1,200, 12 x $250 = $3,000) = $3,000, line 3 = $3,000 and line 6 = min($3,000, $45,000, $3,000) = $3,000, which is EXACTLY what the unrestricted graph computes. On this return the primary filer's deemed income was never binding, so the flush text costs the taxpayer nothing and this refusal was containing nothing. Pinned rather than argued by tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-overlap-all-months-to-one-spouse-files, which is this fixture plus the two overlap answers and which files at the same $3,000.
THE OVER-CLAIM IS REAL ON A DIFFERENT SHAPE, AND ITS SIZE IS THE WHOLE EXPENSE CAP. The two chains deem INDEPENDENTLY, so the unrestricted graph gives EACH spouse their full month count and both can reach twelve months at once; the statute has only P + S - V months to hand out between them, which is at most twelve, so at most ONE of them can. Measured on the pair tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-overlap-unallocated-both-chains-deem-full-refused and tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-overlap-allocated-balanced-caught, which are the same return twice: MFJ, ONE qualifying person ($250 a month), both spouses students all twelve months so all twelve are shared, $1,000 of wages each, $6,000 of expenses.
UNRESTRICTED, each chain deems 12 x $250 = $3,000, lines 4 and 5 are both $3,000, /lowerOfCdccEarnedIncomeMfj lands EXACTLY on /cdccQualifyingExpenseCap, the strict GreaterThan in /showSpecialEarnedIncomeKnockoutFlowInCredits is FALSE, /knockoutStudentOrDisabled does not fire, and the return files a line-6 base of the whole $3,000 cap. ONLY THIS REFUSAL stops it, which is the sharpest statement of why this refusal exists.
UNDER THE FLUSH TEXT there are twelve months to allocate between two spouses, so the smaller of lines 4 and 5 can never exceed six months at $250 = $1,500 whatever the allocation; at six/six both lines read $1,500, the strict gate goes TRUE and /knockoutStudentOrDisabled refuses the return instead. So the divergence on this shape is not a smaller credit — it is a return that files $3,000 of base where the statute permits no filable Form 2441 at all. Taxpayer-favourable, the direction this repo treats most seriously.
NO LONGER WIDER THAN THE STATUTE ON AN ATTESTED DISJOINT SPLIT — NARROWED 2026-08-04 (loop-4 lane CD2, BUILD-FIRST directive; the prior paragraph is in git history). It used to say that a couple who split the year — one spouse a student January to June, the other July to December — satisfies the flush text exactly and was refused here anyway, because filers:/filers/*/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool is a single Int with no month identity so the graph could not tell a legal split from an illegal overlap, and that "the narrowing is the future unit, not this one". That unit is this one. The body now carries Not(/cdccDeemedMonthsDoNotOverlap), which is true unless the return has BOTH attested a zero overlap (the new Int /cdccMonthsBothSpousesStudentOrDisabled) AND passed the arithmetic check that a zero overlap is possible at all (the two per-filer counts summing to at most twelve). An attested-and-possible disjoint split now files; everything else is refused exactly as before, including — deliberately — every return that simply leaves the overlap question unanswered.
WHY THE RELEASE IS SAFE, STATED AS THE BOUND IT ACTUALLY IS. THE FIRST DRAFT OF THIS PARAGRAPH CLAIMED MORE AND WAS FALSIFIED BY A FIXTURE BEFORE IT SHIPPED: it said that on every released return NO DEEMED DOLLAR IS ENTERED. That was wrong, and the shape that broke it — six months each with isStudent and isDisabled false on both filers — is now refused by conjunct (3) on /cdccDeemedMonthsDoNotOverlap rather than argued away. The corrected bound, and the arithmetic it rests on:
Write r for the monthly rate and C for /cdccQualifyingExpenseCap; the cap is EXACTLY twelve times the rate in both configurations ($250/$3,000 and $500/$6,000). A released return has both month counts at least 1 and summing to at most 12, so neither spouse's deemed product can exceed 11r, which is strictly below C. If deeming BINDS on either chain, that chain's Form 2441 line is at most 11r, so /lowerOfCdccEarnedIncomeMfj is at most 11r and the strict GreaterThan in /showSpecialEarnedIncomeKnockoutFlowInCredits is TRUE. Conjunct (3) guarantees the other precondition of that gate — /specialEarnedIncomeFlowRequirementsSansIncomeAndFilingStatus is Any(the two filers' isStudentOrDisabled), and both are true on a released return. So the student/disabled screens ALWAYS show on a released return where deeming binds, and /knockoutStudentOrDisabled then turns on the taxpayer's own made-less-than-the-monthly-amount answers, which a filer whose annual earned income falls below their own deemed product answers yes.
THE HONEST FORM OF THE BOUND is therefore: a released return on which deeming binds is refused by /knockoutStudentOrDisabled WHENEVER THE MADE-LESS QUESTIONS ARE ANSWERED TRUTHFULLY, and the graph cannot do better than that because those two paths are bare Writables with no IsComplete and no consistency guard (/primaryFilerMadeLessThanDisabledOrStudentMonthlyIncome and its twin). Two residual shapes follow and are named rather than hidden. (i) Both answered FALSE while deeming binds is arithmetically self-contradictory — annual earned income below months times r forces at least one of those months below r — so it is an incoherent answer set, the same class conjunct (3) now refuses on the status question, and it is NOT guarded here. (ii) Both left UNANSWERED makes /knockoutStudentOrDisabled Incomplete rather than true; the flow shows those screens exactly when the gate above is true, so this is a flow-completeness question and not one this refusal can settle. WITNESS FOR THE COMMON CASE, so the bound is pinned and not merely argued: tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-disjoint-split-deeming-binds-caught is released by THIS refusal and refused by /knockoutStudentOrDisabled instead.
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR /knockoutStudentOrDisabled — the taxable-benefits placement and the missing section 21(b)(1)(C) abode test, both taxpayer-favourable. Both need deeming to BIND before they can move a dollar, so they are out of reach on a released return in every case the bound above covers. They are NOT provably out of reach in residual shape (ii). That exposure is not new in kind: the single-deemed-spouse population already files and already carries it. It is disclosed here rather than counted, because no corpus measurement of it was taken. [2026-08-05, loop-8 correction: obligations (e) and (f) LANDED that same day (loop-7 lane CD6, squash 1cd93c88a — the benefits add now sits under its own section 21(d)(2) floor and all four deeming arms carry the abode conjunct), so the exposure this paragraph contains is CLOSED; the paragraph stands as the record of why containment was needed while they were live. The knockout contract's remaining ground is CD6's own both-limbs residual, recorded on the /knockoutStudentOrDisabled contract.]
THE OVERLAPPING POPULATION IS RELEASED TOO WHEN IT ANSWERS — NARROWED AGAIN 2026-08-04 (loop-4 lane CD3; the prior paragraph is in git history). It said that a joint return whose spouses genuinely overlap "is still refused, because allocating the shared months is a different rule". That contract is filled. The body now also carries Not(/cdccOverlappedMonthsValidlyAllocated), and the split it gates is applied to all four deemed arms at once by income:/primaryFilerDeemedMonthsAfterOverlapAllocation and its twin, which the two deemed products read.
WHAT IS STILL REFUSED, AND WHY THIS REFUSAL DOES NOT RETIRE. Both months answered above zero, and neither release proved: the overlap count unanswered, or the allocation unanswered, or an answer set that cannot describe a real calendar (more shared months than one spouse had, more allocated than shared, or a union above twelve months), or a return that will not say both spouses were students or unable to care for themselves. Retiring it would deem both chains in full for a return that never answered the overlap questions, which is the over-claim; refusing to deem AT ALL for that return instead would file a $0-or-tiny Form 2441 line 19 and silently UNDER-claim, which obligation (a) named as strictly worse. There is no third option that files, so the refusal is permanent for the unanswered population and this is the narrowest it can be.
TYPE/SIGN/ROUNDING: Boolean; no rounding. COMPLETE-SAFE AND INERT ON THE WHOLE CORPUS: both months writables are unanswered on every scenario and every node-test fixture except the ones this cluster authored, and MEASURED on this branch, ZERO scenarios answer BOTH. The isFilingStatusMFJ conjunct is first and the two IsCompletes precede the two comparisons, so a non-MFJ return and an MFJ return with unanswered months both resolve false without evaluating anything else. flow:/flowIsKnockedOut already depends on filingStatus:/isFilingStatusMFJ through /knockoutStudentOrDisabled, so this adds no new completeness exposure there. BOTH NARROWING CONJUNCTS KEEP THAT INERTNESS: /cdccDeemedMonthsDoNotOverlap and /cdccOverlappedMonthsValidlyAllocated each open with an IsComplete over a writable no corpus file answers, so each is false-and-Complete everywhere and Not(it) is true everywhere — this refusal's value is unchanged on every scenario in the corpus and on every node-test fixture that does not answer the two new Ints.

Whether to knock out a tp who (or whose spouse) was a student or disabled based on earned income rule.
THIS REFUSAL DOES NOT COVER THE BOTH-SPOUSES SHAPE, and the reason is arithmetic: its credits gate /showSpecialEarnedIncomeKnockoutFlowInCredits is GreaterThan(/cdccQualifyingExpenseCap, /lowerOfCdccEarnedIncomeMfj), and full-year deeming lands EXACTLY on that cap ($3,000 with one qualifying person, $6,000 with two or more), so the strict comparison goes false and this fact evaporates. That gap is refused separately by /knockoutBothSpousesDeemedStudentOrDisabled, which carries the full statement.
===================================================================================== WHAT THIS REFUSAL IS FOR.
THIS REFUSAL WAS NEVER ABOUT STUDENTS OR DISABILITY. It was about a computation this dictionary could not do correctly. Section 21(d)(2) deems a student or incapacitated filer to have earned at least $250 a month ($500 with two or more qualifying persons), and the printed rule is MONTH BY MONTH: for each qualifying month take the higher of the rate or that month's actual earnings, and for every other month take actual earnings. This graph computed a year-level shortcut, max(annual, months x rate), and the shortcut is not the rule. So rather than file a wrong number, the return was refused.
THREE DEVIATIONS WERE CONTAINED HERE, ALL THREE NOW COMPUTED: - THE ANNUAL-VERSUS-MONTHLY UNDER-STATEMENT (the contract's obligation (b)). The shortcut is a LOWER BOUND on the correct figure — for any month set and any monthly earnings, correct is at least the annual sum and at least months x rate — so given a correct month count the shipped figure could only ever be too LOW, always a smaller credit, always taxpayer-ADVERSE. Closed by income:/{primary,secondary}FilerCdccDeemedOrExactFigure on the credit side and .../ForBenefits on the exclusion side. - THE BOTH-LIMBS RESIDUAL. Section 21(d)(2)'s disjunction is asymmetric: a STUDENT month deems on its own, but an incapacity month deems only if the filer also shared the taxpayer's abode more than half the year (section 21(b)(1)(C)). One conflated months count could not express that, so a both-limbs filer whose abode test failed deemed on every answered month. Closed by the per-limb partition in filers.xml feeding income:/{primary,secondary}FilerCdccQualifyingMonths. - THE UNANSWERED-STUDENT LEAK (the contract's item 2). The limb conjunct reads an unanswered isStudent as a definite NO, so a filer could answer the months, resolve a Complete deemed product, and still fall through to their actual earned income silently. Covered by the completeness terms inside /{primary,secondary}FilerCdccFigureIsExact.
SO THE REFUSAL NOW ASKS THE ONE QUESTION THAT WAS ALWAYS THE POINT: is this filer's figure APPROXIMATE? It fires where income:/{primary,secondary}FilerCdccFigureIsExact is false and that filer attests they earned less than the deemed amount in some qualifying month — and it stands down where the figure is exact, because there is then nothing wrong to contain. A filer who answers the section 21(d)(2) questions now FILES.
THE SECOND OPERAND IS TWO All's RATHER THAN AN Any OF TWO ATTESTATIONS, which is the contract's item 4 and is required rather than cosmetic: each filer's exactness must be paired with THAT filer's own attestation. A single global term would either over-refuse (a return where one spouse is exact and the other is not) or under-refuse (the mirror).
THE SECOND CONJUNCT'S ARMS EACH OPEN ON THEIR OWN FILER'S MEMBERSHIP, 2026-09-02, and it is a COMPLETENESS REPAIR rather than a population change. The arm for a filer now reads All(Any(filers:/<filer>/isStudentOrDisabled, Not(IsComplete(that same fact))), that filer's attestation, Not(that filer's exactness)) — "this filer is in the section 21(d)(2) population, OR we do not yet know that they are not". WHY IT WAS NEEDED: this module's own completeness gate /disabledOrStudentFlowIsComplete requires an answer to /primaryFilerMadeLessThanDisabledOrStudentMonthlyIncome ONLY where filers:/primaryFiler/isStudentOrDisabled holds, and /showEarnedIncomeRuleTp2 offers the spouse's question on the same condition — so on the ordinary return where exactly one spouse is a student or is disabled, the OTHER spouse's attestation is never asked. The unanswered writable made its All() Incomplete, the Any() Incomplete and this whole refusal Incomplete, on a return the flow itself calls complete. MEASURED on the one committed corpus scenario that answers a single attestation, scenarios/upstream/ cdcc-mfj-filer-qp-multiple-qps (MFJ, the SECOND-listed filer disabled, only the secondary's attestation answered and answered false, /showSpecialEarnedIncomeKnockoutFlowInCredits TRUE): before this unit /knockoutStudentOrDisabled never resolved; after it the fact reads Complete false. flow:/flowIsKnockedOut is Placeholder false on that return either way, so NO dollar and NO filing outcome moves and no committed row moves — the whole 704-scenario spine and all 84 form2441 cases are byte-identical. THE NARROWING IS ALSO CORRECT ON THE MERITS AND NOT MERELY CONVENIENT: a filer who is neither a student nor disabled has no section 21(d)(2) qualifying month, nothing about their figure is deemed, and their figure is their actual earned income exactly — so a TRUE attestation from them is a contradiction and refusing on it was over-refusal.
WHY THE MEMBERSHIP CONJUNCT IS Any(membership, Not(IsComplete(membership))) AND NOT THE BARE DEPENDENCY, 2026-09-02: filers:/filers/*/isStudentOrDisabled is Any(../isStudent, ../isDisabled) over two bare writables with no Placeholder and no default, so it is INCOMPLETE whenever one limb is answered false and the other is unanswered. A bare conjunct therefore made the All() Incomplete on exactly that store — and the first draft of this edit did. MEASURED on scenarios/upstream/cdcc-mfj-filer-qp-multiple-qps with the primary's isDisabled removed and /primaryFilerMadeLessThanDisabledOrStudentMonthlyIncome answered true: at f83e07d2d the return was REFUSED (/knockoutStudentOrDisabled Complete true, flow:/flowIsKnockedOut Complete true); with the bare conjunct the guard stopped resolving, flow:/flowIsKnockedOut fell to Placeholder false and /cdccSectionIsComplete stayed Complete true — i.e. a return the tree used to refuse became SUBMITTABLE with an unresolved knockout. The Any() restores the pre-unit refusal wherever membership is unknown and keeps the whole narrowing wherever it is known. IsComplete is total, so the Any() is never Incomplete; and this is NOT the forbidden IsComplete-on-a-complete-safe-fact pattern, because the fact is not complete-safe, the test is negated, and it is one arm of a disjunction rather than the fact's own answered-ness standing in for a source-answered predicate. Pinned by tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-membership-unknown-still-refused. THE HONEST STATEMENT OF THE NARROWING'S DIRECTION, replacing the first draft's "it can only refuse fewer returns": as landed it refuses fewer returns ONLY where membership is known false, and it refuses exactly as before wherever membership is unknown.
THE RESIDUE THIS REFUSAL KEEPS, NAMED because a narrowing that cannot name its residue must not land: a filer who IS a student or is disabled, who attests they earned less than the deemed rate in some qualifying month, and who has NOT answered the four section 21(d)(2) intake writables in filers.xml — so their figure is still the max(annual, months x rate) approximation. That is a DATA-COMPLETENESS residue and it is the correct permanent refusal: there is no default this dictionary could invent for the per-month decomposition that would not be a derivation. It ends per return when the intake is answered, not by a dictionary edit. Witnessed by tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/ cdcc-deemed-intake-unanswered-residue-refused, which is the same return as cdcc-deemed-income-student-spouse with the non-student filer's attestation removed: the student spouse attests, the intake is unanswered, this fact is Complete TRUE and flow:/flowIsKnockedOut is Complete true.
WHAT IS STILL NOT MODELLED, kept from the contract because it did not land with it: the line 1b Conservation Reserve Program subtraction, the Part II farm and nonfarm OPTIONAL METHODS (whose direction the instructions themselves call indeterminate), and the per-filer attribution of a return-level Schedule F. None of them is contained by this refusal; each is disclosed on its own fact. =====================================================================================
THE ATTESTATION WRITABLES STAY, AND THE REASON CHANGED — READ THIS BEFORE PROPOSING THEIR DELETION AGAIN. /{primary,secondary}FilerMadeLessThanDisabledOrStudentMonthlyIncome were put up for retirement on 2026-08-07 as dead weight: they ask the filer to compare their earnings against a deemed amount no screen has shown them, which is a tax conclusion rather than a fact, and filers:/filers/*/cdccEarnedOverDeemedRateInAnyQualifyingMonth is the same question with the polarity that makes the figure computable. Checking before deleting reversed the conclusion.
A FALSE ANSWER HERE IS A THIRD EXACTNESS CONDITION, not a dead question. "Made LESS than the deemed amount in any qualifying month" answered FALSE means every qualifying month cleared the rate. Then each of those months contributes its own actual earnings rather than the floor, the remaining months contribute theirs, and the correct figure is simply the ANNUAL earned income — which is exactly what the pre-stage max(annual, months x rate) shortcut returns, because annual dominates months x rate on that population. So the graph has always computed these returns correctly, and the refusal has always correctly stood down on them. Verified over 20,000 randomised month vectors.
AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE END OF THE SAME COMPARISON from the new screening question, which is why neither writable subsumes the other: this one certifies every qualifying month was AT OR ABOVE the rate (exact via the shortcut), the new one certifies every qualifying month was AT OR BELOW it (exact via the months-times-rate identity). Deleting this pair would have withdrawn a population this dictionary can already file — an over-refusal regression dressed up as cleanup.
NOT LIFTED INTO income:/{primary,secondary}FilerCdccFigureIsExact, and that was tried: these are cdcc Writables with no Export, so income.xml cannot depend on them, and the runner rejects the dictionary outright. The arm would also have been inert — inside this refusal's All(attestation, Not(exact)), a false attestation already short-circuits, so the condition can never change an outcome. It is recorded here as prose instead, which is where a reader deciding whether to delete the writable will actually look.
WHAT IS ACTUALLY LEFT, 2026-09-02, stated because the records contract at /filers/*/cdccMonthlyEarnedIncomeUnderSection21d2 says the successor is a MISSING INPUT and that is no longer true. The input SHIPS, as four writables in filers.xml — /filers/*/cdccEarnedOverDeemedRateInAnyQualifyingMonth (the screening Boolean), /filers/*/cdccEarnedIncomeDuringQualifyingMonths, /filers/*/cdccQualifyingMonthsOverDeemedRate and /filers/*/cdccEarnedIncomeInMonthsOverDeemedRate — and income:/{primary,secondary}- FilerCdccFigureIsExact reads exactly those. What is missing is the SCREEN: no application asks them yet, so the population this refusal contains is never actually offered the questions that would release it. That is arm (A) of the /flowKnockoutBenefitsDistribution pattern — discharged by the application asking, not by a dictionary edit.
AND THERE IS A SECOND, DICTIONARY-SIDE ARM, 2026-09-02. THE CLOSED FORM IS NOT EXACT ACROSS A SET BOUNDARY. The four intake writables are keyed on the filer's OWN reported student-or-incapacity months (call that set S — see the Description of filers:/filers/*/cdccEarnedIncomeDuringQualifyingMonths, "earned DURING the months they were a full-time student or unable to care for themself": no abode gate, no overlap split). The deemed term enters the exact arms through income:/{primary,secondary}FilerIncomeForMonthsDisabledOrInSchool, which is DeemedMonthsAfterOverlapAllocation x rate and therefore counts only the ABODE-GATED, OVERLAP-ALLOCATED months (call that set D). D is a subset of S, strictly, whenever an incapacity month fails the section 21(b)(1)(C) abode test or a shared month is allocated to the other spouse. For a month in S but not in D the statute says the month contributes ACTUAL earnings; the tree removes those earnings once via (annual - E_N) and never adds them back, because the deemed term covers only D. The error is exactly E_S - E_D and it is always taxpayer-adverse. THE IDENTITY IS EXACT WHEN, AND ONLY WHEN, filers:/filers/*/cdccMonthsDisabledOrInSchool equals that filer's income:/*FilerDeemedMonthsAfterOverlapAllocation. Nothing gates the exact arms or income:/*FilerCdccFigureIsExact on that equality today, and THIS REFUSAL DOES NOT CONTAIN IT: on such a return the intake is answered, so FigureIsExact is true, this guard stands Complete false and the return FILES understated. MEASURED at f83e07d2d and unchanged by this unit (a pre-existing defect dating to the 2026-08-07 KO5 discharge, not a regression): tests/nodes/ty2025/form2441/cdcc-deemed-per-limb-partition-closes-residual (2 student months and 4 abode-failed incapacity months, cdccQualifyingPerson false, W-2 wages 1,200, rate 250) plus the two intake answers cdccEarnedOverDeemedRateInAnyQualifyingMonth false and cdccEarnedIncomeDuringQualifyingMonths 300.00 prints /cdccEarnedIncomeLine5 1,400.00 and /cdccTotalCredit 280.00 where the statute gives 1,700 and 340 if the 300 fell in the four abode-failed months (2 x 250 deemed + 1,200 actual): a 300-dollar line-5 and 60-dollar credit under-statement on a return that files. The narrowest fix is an income.xml unit gating the two exact arms and FigureIsExact on that month-set equality and falling back to the pre-stage approximation otherwise; it is out of this unit's grant and is handed up as a seat:build / tax-law issue.
